processing: Coarse, stemmy leaf is fixed, rolled, sun-dried, re-fried and re-rolled, then piled and sun-dried. This is the base material for pressing Hubei green brick.
harvest_season: Little is recorded about a prized picking; it is judged by storage age rather than season.
appearance_dry: Dense, even dark brown to black-brown, usually pressed into hard bricks.
taste_profile: Thick, soft and mellow, with an aged aroma and touches of old wood, earth and sometimes honey that grow with storage.

brewing.notes: Clay or porcelain; water at 95 to 100 °C and about 20 to 30 seconds to begin, lengthening each steep.

vintage_note: Sold by storage age, and the value lies in years: sellers describe lots kept for decades. Younger bricks are for everyday drinking and for keeping. Ask for the production year, as age is the main thing you are paying for and hard to verify.
description:
Lao qing cha, literally 'old green tea', is the name used in southern Hubei for the dark tea of Chibi, Xianning, Tongshan, Chongyang and Tongcheng. Strictly it is the base material pressed into qing zhuan, though the name overlaps with qing zhuan and chuan zi cha, and one tea site treats them as the same.

What it stresses is time. Fermentation runs long and storage longer, so the aged character becomes the point, and it behaves very differently from what the word 'qing' might suggest to someone who knows green tea.

The cup pours red-brown, soft and thick, with old wood and earth and a little honey in good lots. Boil the water, begin with 20 to 30 seconds, and lengthen as you go; aged notes come forward over several steeps.

The usual tea-shop health claims for it, from weight loss to fighting cancer, should be taken lightly. Buy it for the flavour, and buy an inexpensive young brick alongside an older one to see what storage really does.
history:
Little is documented about the name itself as distinct from Hubei brick tea generally. The growing counties named above are the same area that produced the region's green bricks, and its wider history belongs with Hubei dark tea and Yangloudong brick tea.

Chinese tea references list it under dark teas alongside Fu brick, Liubao and others; a detailed history under this exact name is thin.
